And the Sultan demanded of him ten thousand thousands of dinars (ten million),
that he might ransom himself with them.
And the King said:
"Even if I gave the whole kingdom of the Romans,
it would be small in comparison with saving my life.
However, the treasuries {OCR?} of the kingdom of the Romans have been much depleted
since I became king,
by the armies that I have employed."
And an agreement was reached:
that he should give one thousand thousand dinars (one million) as the price of his life,
and each year three hundred and sixty thousand dinars of tribute.
And the Sultan commanded,
and they loosed the irons from him,
and he seated him on his throne, the one which he had captured from him,
and they ate and drank together.
And the Sultan demanded of him Antioch, Edessa, Hierapolis (Mabbug), and Manzikert, which the Romans had taken from the Arabs.
And the King answered and said:
"When I return to my kingdom,
you send an army and make war upon them,
and I will send word to them that they surrender.
Otherwise, now, even if I send word,
they will not listen to me."
And the King said to the Sultan:
"Henceforth, if you wish to send me away, send me quickly,
before the Romans set up a king for themselves,
and then I will not be able to fulfill even one of these things."
And this indeed happened.
And the Sultan commanded,
and made to ride with him one hundred slaves and two emirs,
to go with him to Constantinople.
And the Sultan himself also escorted him for about one parasang.
And when he wished to turn back,
the King wished to dismount,
but the Sultan adjured him not to dismount.
And so, while mounted, they kissed one another,
and separated.
For thus we have found this narrative in two copies (sources):
Arabic and Persian.
The blessed Mar Michael, however, wrote:
that the Sultan's sister's son captured the King,
and another Turk came and killed the Sultan's sister's son,
and took the King for himself,
so that the bounty would be his.
And that when the Sultan asked the King:
"What was in your intention to do with me,
if I had fallen into your hands?" Diogenes answered:
"I would have wished to burn you in fire."
And it is clear
that an uncouth word like this would not have been spoken by a king to a king;
nor would a Turk have been able to kill the Sultan's sister's son,
and snatch the King from his hands.
